actuation: Two rotational electric actuators (7 Nm DC servo motors M1 and M2)
Tendon-pulley-slider mechanism translating M2 rotation into linear displacement along the wrist axis
Non-stretchable / inelastic tendon driving the fingers
constitutive_assumptions: Tendon is perfectly inelastic and non-stretchable
Shear deformation of the rigid rod is negligible
Integrated compression spring exhibits ideal linear elasticity with constant K
Friction between the rigid rod and holding pins is neglected in the dynamic model formulation
Grasp stiffness is modeled as the partial derivative of applied tendon force with respect to displacement
Cumulative disturbance and modeling uncertainties (unmodeled friction, object stiffness variations, contact dynamics) are bounded
control_variables: Sliding mode control gain Gamma (set to 220 deg/s in experiments)
Error convergence rate eta (arbitrary positive constant, set to 20 in experiments)
Quasi-sliding mode control input omega_R (rotational velocity of the shaft of motor M2)
Inner-loop anti-windup PI controller gains (KP, KI, Kaw, and conversion gain Kbeta)
Motor M1 shaft rotation angle theta bounded in [0, pi/2]
dependent_variables: Tendon displacement d under applied external force
Compression of the linear spring Zs'
Apparent output stiffness of the hand/fingers delta_o
Actual angular motion/trajectory of the fingers and tracking error
Grip force Fg exerted on grasped objects
Mechanical hysteresis band width during loading-unloading cycles
Peak magnitude of finger motion in frequency response Bode plots
Sliding variable sigma and sliding surface reaching time Ts

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Coupling an object with unknown stiffness to a robotic gripper can shift system poles into the right half-plane and induce grasp instability, which can be mitigated by introducing passive compliance into the actuation system.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Theoretical modeling and root locus analysis

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The apparent stiffness of the robotic hand is analytically governed by the angle between the tendon and the spring-loaded rod, varying from the linear spring constant K when parallel up to theoretically infinite stiffness when perpendicular.
Static force-displacement characterization demonstrates that tendon elongation for a given applied tensile force decreases monotonically as the rod angle theta increases from 5 to 55 degrees.
Increasing finger stiffness via the variable stiffness mechanism improves trajectory tracking accuracy under sinusoidal inputs and reduces the peak magnitude in frequency response Bode plots.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Dynamic trajectory tracking and frequency analysis experiments

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The robotic hand exhibits mechanical hysteresis during cyclic tendon loading and unloading, but the hysteresis band narrows as the rod angle theta increases.

A first-order sliding mode controller combined with an inner anti-windup PI velocity loop converges error states to zero in finite time and achieves stable grip force tracking across objects of varying stiffness with small steady-state error and zero or negligible overshoot.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Robotic control experiment on hardware testbed

experimental_setup: VSH1 robotic hand prototypes with 3 fingers / 6 joints and 2 fingers / 2 joints actuated by two 7 Nm DC servo motors
Tensile characterization rig using hung deadweights to measure tendon elongation d across various rod angles theta with a 0.3 N/mm spring
Trajectory tracking setup comprising a sinusoidal motion input to motor M2, a rigid fire brick obstacle, a rotational joint encoder, and a Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR)
Hysteresis testing rig using gradual loading and unloading of external force on a 0.55 N/mm spring across discrete rod angles
Two-finger VSH1 mounted as an end-effector on an ABB IRB 1200 6-axis industrial robot (7 kg payload)
Custom Variable Stiffness Object (VSO) testbed with interchangeable compression springs (Kb = 1.0, 1.25, 2.6, and 3.3 N/mm) and a linear potentiometer sampled via an Arduino Mega (9600 bps)
future_work: Redesigning mechanical couplings to minimize friction and damping in order to narrow the mechanical hysteresis band
independent_variables: Rod angle / servo motor M1 angle theta (evaluated at discrete angles from 0 deg to 55 deg)
Applied external tensile force / weight hung on tendon
Stiffness constant K of the integrated linear compression spring (0.3 N/mm and 0.55 N/mm)
Linear distance B between the motor M1 shaft center and the hand wrist axis
Stiffness of the grasped object Kb (1.0, 1.25, 2.6, and 3.3 N/mm in the VSO)
Desired grip force profile Fd (step inputs of increasing amplitude and sinusoidal inputs)
limitations_inferred: Grip force and trajectory tracking evaluations were restricted to planar 1D contact against a stationary block or single-axis spring mechanism, without evaluating multi-finger grasping of arbitrary 3D geometry objects during manipulator motion.
Both finger sets are driven through a single shared rod-spring-tendon mechanism, preventing independent stiffness modulation across individual fingers or individual joints.
The assumption of an inelastic tendon may degrade over extensive cyclic operation due to tendon creep or elasticity, affecting stiffness calibration and force precision.
Mounting motor M1 directly on a translating slider introduces added moving mass and inertia to the linear wrist axis, which may constrain high-speed dynamic response.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The initial prototype displays a noticeable hysteresis band attributable to friction and damping across mechanical couplings.
Friction between the sliding rod and holding pins was neglected in the dynamic model formulation for simplicity.
The stiffness of unknown grasped objects cannot be calculated in advance, making precise model-based grasp modeling inherently inaccurate and necessitating robust control.
System feedback relies on an inexpensive (£9) 1D Force Sensing Resistor (FSR) with variable resistance rather than a precision multi-axis load cell.
main_results: Derived and validated an analytical closed-form model relating tendon force, displacement, spring constant, and rod angle theta, showing stiffness increases monotonically with theta.
Demonstrated a broad stiffness variation range from the minimum spring rate K (at theta = 0 deg) up to very stiff behavior approaching 90 deg perpendicularity.
Showed experimentally that increasing the mechanism stiffness stabilizes trajectory tracking under sinusoidal disturbance inputs and attenuates dynamic resonance peaks in Bode plots.
Identified that mechanical hysteresis is angle-dependent, narrowing as rod angle theta increases.

Successfully demonstrated robust force tracking on an industrial manipulator across diverse object stiffnesses (1.0 to 3.3 N/mm) using a hybrid PI-sliding mode controller, achieving finite-time convergence of the sliding variable, negligible overshoot, and steady-state errors that decrease at higher stiffness settings.
modeling_methods: Kinematic and geometric modeling using the law of sines to formulate spring compression and tendon displacement relationships
Grasp stiffness derivation through partial differentiation of applied tendon force with respect to displacement
Second-order lumped parameter electromechanical dynamic modeling of the robotic hand and DC servo motor system
First-order sliding mode controller (FSMC) design using a quasi-sliding mode saturation function coupled with an inner anti-windup PI velocity feedback loop
Lyapunov stability and reachability analysis under bounded cumulative system disturbances and uncertainties
performance_metrics: Stiffness tuning range (from baseline spring stiffness K up to near-rigid stiffness)
Trajectory tracking error under sinusoidal motion input Sin(5t)
Grip force tracking accuracy (steady-state error and percent overshoot under step and sinusoidal reference forces)
Mechanical hysteresis band width across loading-unloading cycles
Sliding manifold reaching time Ts and finite-time error convergence to zero
Peak magnitude attenuation in frequency response Bode plots
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrates that a broad range of variable stiffness can be realized using only two standard servo motors and a single linear compression spring, demonstrating an alternative to complex multi-actuator antagonistic systems.

Shows that combining passive serial compliance with robust sliding mode control allows stable grip force regulation on unknown stiffness objects even when using low-cost, low-accuracy tactile sensors.

Highlights that mechanical hysteresis arising from friction and mechanical couplings is a key limiting factor in tendon-driven variable stiffness actuators that requires careful mechanical optimization.
paper.research_objective: To design, model, and experimentally evaluate an affordable, durable, adaptable, and compliant variable stiffness robotic hand (VSH1) for industrial applications that provides a wide stiffness adjustment range, low hysteresis, rapid impedance control, and robust grip force regulation under object uncertainties.
paper.research_problem: Robotic grasping of objects with unknown dynamic properties and mechanical parameters easily becomes unstable under conventional fixed-gain control, while existing compliant and variable stiffness grippers often suffer from design complexity, small force/stiffness operating ranges, high cost, weight, and durability limitations in industrial environments.
stiffness_mechanism: tendon-rod-spring configuration with a single linear compression spring and rigid sliding rod
paper.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
